analysis.one_liner: Pays landowners when endangered-species rules cut their property value and eases many species-protection rules.
analysis.headline: The House Resources Committee approved it 27-17, but the bill sat on the House calendar and never got a floor vote before Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the Endangered Species Act to weigh economic impacts and property rights alongside species survival. If federal protection cut a property's value by 20% or more, taxpayers would have to pay the owner; landowners could also demand buyouts and sue for legal fees. It narrows what counts as illegally 'harming' a species, exempts routine farming, ranching, and road-maintenance work, makes it harder to list species and easier to delist them, shifts several burdens of proof onto federal scientists, and lets federal power users and shrimp trawlers off the hook for part of their compliance costs.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of land restricted by species protections — from family farm and ranch owners to large developers — gain a right to compensation or buyout at taxpayer expense. Timber, agriculture, real estate, and energy interests gain broad new exemptions from species rules, easier permitting, guaranteed 'no surprises' lock-ins, and shifted burdens of proof in federal reviews.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Developers, landowners, timber, farm and energy interests

how_it_helps.text: Requires the federal government to compensate any owner whose property loses 20% or more of its value due to an agency action under the Act, and to buy the affected portion outright if the loss exceeds 50%, with attorney's fees and interest paid to owners who win in court [S2][S4].

Reduces enforcement risk for everyday land uses: an activity is not an illegal 'take' if it is incidental to routine maintenance of pipelines, roads, and rights-of-way, emergency repairs, or public-health actions [S3][S4].

Restricts critical habitat designations on private land unless the owner consents in writing or is compensated, and bars releases of experimental populations on non-federal land without the owner's written consent, with removal on request within 90 days [S3].
Requires federal agencies to pay half the direct compliance costs of conservation plans borne by non-federal parties and federal power marketing administrations in the Pacific Northwest [S3].

Adds incentives for landowners: habitat conservation grants, technical assistance, faster permits for low-impact activities, and guarantees that parties complying with approved plans face no new restrictions or payments later [S2][S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through agency appropriations and the new trust fund, bear compensation payments, buyouts, attorney's fees, interest, and cost-sharing with utilities and power users. The public also bears the loss of species and habitat protections: the definition of illegal 'harm' shrinks to actions that directly kill or injure an identifiable animal, listing decisions must weigh future voluntary conservation plans, the government must prove species and habitat are actually present before a review can restrict a project, and congressionally listed 'population segments' must be re-approved or delisted [S2][S3][S4].

drawbacks.text: The compensation guarantee is funded only if Congress appropriates the money each year; agencies would otherwise have to divert operating funds, meaning species protection could stall while budgets are fought over [S4].

Redefining 'harm' to cover only direct killing or injury of an identifiable animal would remove protection for habitat destruction — the main driver of extinction — because harming habitat without touching an animal would no longer be illegal [S2][S3][S4].

The bill bars federal scientists from issuing a 'jeopardy' opinion based on insufficient data and places on them the burden of proving a species or its critical habitat is actually present where a project would act — hard-to-prove standards that let projects proceed when information is uncertain [S3].

Compensation for large landholdings and buyouts at pre-restriction value would be paid from public funds, so taxpayers would effectively underwrite continued development of habitat that the public is trying to save [S4].

A new bar on informal agency determinations — no policy, guideline, or finding can be used unless it goes through full proposed-rulemaking with 60 days of comment — would slow emergency protections and routine enforcement [S2][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's fairer core — compensating small landowners, grants, faster low-impact permits, and 'no surprises' certainty for people who plan in good faith — addresses a real weakness of the Endangered Species Act, which regulates private land without paying for it. But the same protections are written broadly enough to cover large landholders and resource industries, and they are paired with changes that would hollow out protection itself: habitat harm decriminalized, listing decisions complicated, burden of proof shifted to the government, and delisting made easier. On balance, the bill's main effect would have been a large shift of species-protection costs onto taxpayers and a weaker safety net for wildlife, with genuine but secondary benefits for cooperating landowners.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the Resources Committee and was printed on the House calendar in September 1996, but the House never debated or voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced September 7, 1995 by Rep. Don Young of Alaska with 100-plus original cosponsors; 128 members signed on in total, 111 Republicans and 17 Democrats [S4][S5].
The Natural Resources Committee held hearings and marked it up in October 1995, ordering it reported amended by a 27-17 vote [S6].
It was reported amended on September 9, 1996 as House Report 104-778, the Agriculture Committee was discharged, and it was placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 420 [S6].
No floor action followed; the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the Endangered Species Act was left unreauthorized but still in force [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Endangered species and the public's existing wildlife protections, which remained intact because the rollback never came to a vote; the Act kept its stronger protections even though its formal reauthorization had lapsed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Species protections survived; the bill died on the calendar

for.name: Rep. Don Young
for.role: U.S. Representative (R-AK), sponsor and chairman of the House Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through his committee, which ordered it reported amended by a 27-17 vote in October 1995 and reported it in September 1996.

for.name: Rep. Richard Pombo
for.role: U.S. Representative (R-CA), original cosponsor and lead House advocate for rewriting the Endangered Species Act
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor of the bill and its most visible floor advocate.

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: The administration opposed the bill and backed its own less sweeping ESA reauthorization, dimming prospects for a floor vote in an election year.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote after it was reported and placed on the Union Calendar in September 1996, and it died when the Congress ended.

against.name: U.S. Senate
against.role: The full Senate of the 104th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never took up or acted on the companion effort, leaving the House bill with no path to law.

against.name: Conservation organizations
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the bill as a rollback of species protections and worked to keep it off the floor.

against.name: Clinton administration (Interior Department)
against.what_they_did: Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt promoted administrative ESA reforms and the administration's own reauthorization plan as the alternative to the Young bill.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Republican — 111 of 128 cosponsors were Republicans, joined by 17 mostly conservative and rural Democrats — and the committee reported it 27-17 on a party-tilted vote; opposition organized around the Democratic administration and conservation groups.

industries.industry: Real estate development and large private landholders
industries.note: Compensation or buyout whenever protection cuts property value 20% or more, owner consent required for critical habitat, and a narrowed 'harm' definition would free up land for development at public expense. Ordinary rural landowners share in the compensation benefit, but the largest gains go to owners of the most valuable restricted land.

Routine maintenance, road and right-of-way work, and emergency repairs are exempted from the take prohibition, and state water allocation is shielded from federal restriction. These are the activities most often constrained by species rules.

industries.industry: Electric utilities and Pacific Northwest power users
industries.note: The federal treasury would pay half the direct costs of complying with Columbia River basin conservation plans, shifting a major share of salmon-protection costs from power ratepayers and utilities to taxpayers.

Operators could be exempted from mandatory turtle excluder devices if they instead fund approved conservation programs, loosening the main protection for sea turtles in the Gulf and Atlantic fisheries.

industries.industry: Wildlife trade, falconry, and trophy hunting
industries.note: Imports of threatened species for sport hunting, falconry, captive breeding, and scientific collection would face a presumption of benefit, and the government could not refuse or limit such imports without published substantial evidence to the contrary.

industries.industry: Endangered-species conservation and the public's natural heritage
industries.note: Weakened habitat protection, narrowed harm rules, slower emergency listings, and easier delisting would leave fewer species protected; once a species is gone, the loss is permanent for everyone.
